title: Point first
rule: Say your main point in the first sentence.

examples.work: The client said yes. We start on Monday.
examples.everyday: I'll be late. My train is stuck at Dadar.

insteadOf: So we had the call, and then the client said a few things, and…
analogy: A newspaper headline: you read it first, the details come after.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks, "How did the client call go?" It went well. Answer in two sentences.
answer: It went well. They agreed to the new timeline.
credit: Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle); BLUF (US Army writing standard)

title: Why the point goes first
rule: Give the point first, so people know what the details are for.

examples.work: We need one more week. Here's why: the vendor changed the design.
examples.everyday: Let's eat at home tonight. The fridge is full and it's raining.

insteadOf: First let me give you some background on the vendor situation…
analogy: A train board shows the destination first, then the stops on the way.
tryPrompt: A friend asks, "Are you coming to the wedding?" You are, but late. Say it point first.
answer: Yes, I'm coming, but late. My flight lands at eight.
credit: Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle)

title: The one-line test
rule: Before you speak, say your point to yourself in one line.

examples.work: In one line: the release is ready for Friday.
examples.everyday: In one line: the AC needs a new part, not a new machine.

insteadOf: There are a few things about the release I wanted to mention…
analogy: Like telling the auto driver the place before you explain the shortcut.
tryPrompt: Think of one thing you did at work today. Say it in one line, under ten words.
answer: I fixed the login bug that blocked testing.
credit: Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle)

title: Point first in messages
rule: In messages too, the first line carries the point.

examples.work: Can we move the review to 4 pm? I'm stuck on a client call.
examples.everyday: Dinner's at eight at Amma's place. Bring the sweets from the shop.

insteadOf: Hi, hope you're doing well. I was going through the deck yesterday and…
analogy: A courier label: the name and address go on top, not inside the box.
tryPrompt: You need a colleague's file by noon. Say the first line of your message.
answer: Could you send me the sales file by noon?
credit: BLUF (US Army writing standard)

title: Your turn: point first
rule: Start with the answer; add one reason only if they need it.

examples.work: Yesterday was productive. I finished the pricing page.
examples.everyday: The trip was great. We finally saw the sunrise at Nandi Hills.

insteadOf: Yesterday was… I mean, there was a lot going on, and I had meetings…
analogy: Serve the main dish first; the chutney can come after.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "How was your weekend?" Answer point first about your real weekend, in two sentences.
answer: Relaxing. I slept in and watched a match with my brother.
credit: Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle)

title: Yes or no comes first
rule: If they ask a yes-or-no question, start with yes or no.

examples.work: "Is the demo ready?" "No, not yet. It'll be ready by three."
examples.everyday: "Did you book the tickets?" "Yes, done. Two seats for Saturday."

insteadOf: "Is the demo ready?" "Well, we had some data issues, and then…"
analogy: An umpire's finger: out or not out, before any replay.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks, "Did you send the report?" You haven't. Answer honestly in two sentences.
answer: Not yet. I'll send it by four.

title: A "when" question gets a time
rule: Asked "when"? Give the time or the date first.

examples.work: "When will it be done?" "Thursday evening, if testing goes well."
examples.everyday: "When will you get here?" "In twenty minutes. I'm near the flyover."

insteadOf: "When will it be done?" "It depends on a few things, like testing…"
analogy: A railway announcement gives the platform and the time, not the train's history.
tryPrompt: A friend asks when you're free this week. Answer with the day first.
answer: Saturday evening works. I'm busy till Friday.

title: A "how many" question gets a number
rule: Asked "how many" or "how long"? Say the number first.

examples.work: "How many signed up?" "Forty. That's double last week."
examples.everyday: "How long is the drive?" "About two hours, without traffic."

insteadOf: "How many signed up?" "Quite a lot, actually, more than we expected…"
analogy: A scoreboard shows the runs first; the commentary comes after.
tryPrompt: Someone asks how many hours you worked yesterday. Answer with the number first, then one detail.
answer: About nine. Most of it was meetings.

title: Don't know? Say so first
rule: Not sure? Say so first, then say when you'll know.

examples.work: "Will we launch on time?" "I don't know yet. I'll know by Wednesday."
examples.everyday: "Is the shop open on Sunday?" "Not sure. Let me call and check."

insteadOf: "Will we launch on time?" "So there are many moving parts, and…"
analogy: Like a GPS saying "recalculating" instead of driving you the wrong way.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks if the vendor will deliver on time. You don't know yet. Answer in two sentences.
answer: I'm not sure yet. I'll confirm with them by tomorrow noon.

title: Your turn: answer what they asked
rule: First answer the exact question; then add only what helps.

examples.work: "Can you take this task?" "Yes. I can start after lunch."
examples.everyday: "Did you like the film?" "Loved it. The ending surprised me."

insteadOf: "Did you like the film?" "So the first half was slow, and the songs…"
analogy: A waiter asked for water brings water, not the whole menu.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "Did you finish what you planned today?" Answer about your real day, starting with yes or no.
answer: Mostly, yes. I finished two of my three tasks.

title: One point per sentence
rule: Give each sentence one idea, then start a new one.

examples.work: The client couldn't travel. We moved the meeting to Friday.
examples.everyday: The bus was full. I took an auto instead.

insteadOf: The meeting, which moved because the client couldn't travel, is now Friday.
analogy: One passenger per seat. Squeeze in two and nobody is comfortable.
tryPrompt: Split into two sentences: "I was late because the metro stopped, and that made me miss the stand-up."
answer: The metro stopped. I missed the stand-up.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Break the "and… and…" chain
rule: When you hear yourself say "and" again, stop and start fresh.

examples.work: I fixed two bugs. Then I had the client call.
examples.everyday: We went to the market. Then we had chai at the corner stall.

insteadOf: I did the dashboard and also the meeting and then the client call.
analogy: A long goods train blocks the crossing. Short trains let the traffic through.
tryPrompt: Tell what you did this morning in three short sentences, without joining them with "and".
answer: I woke up at seven. I answered my emails. Then I joined the stand-up.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Keep who and what close
rule: Put who does it right next to what they do.

examples.work: Rahul fixed it. He checked the logs and called the vendor twice.
examples.everyday: My sister cooked dinner. She made dal, rice and two sabzis.

insteadOf: Rahul, after checking the logs and talking to the vendor twice, fixed it.
analogy: Wear the name tag on your shirt, not inside your pocket.
tryPrompt: Make this clearer: "The report, after two rounds of edits and a long review, finally went out."
answer: The report finally went out. It took two rounds of edits and a long review.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Short sentences, steady voice
rule: Short sentences give you a natural place to breathe.

examples.work: We test today. We fix tomorrow. We ship on Friday.
examples.everyday: I'll pick up the cake. You get the candles. The party starts at six.

insteadOf: So the plan is we test today and fix tomorrow and ship on Friday if…
analogy: Each full stop is a station where you can catch your breath.
tryPrompt: Explain your plan for tomorrow in three short sentences, one point each.
answer: I'll finish the slides first. Then I'll meet Priya. I'll leave by six.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Your turn: one point at a time
rule: Say one thing, finish it, then say the next thing.

examples.work: This week was busy. We launched the app on Tuesday.
examples.everyday: My cousin got married on Sunday. The whole family danced till midnight.

insteadOf: My week was busy with the launch and also my cousin's wedding and…
analogy: Pour one cup of chai at a time; don't try to fill three at once.
tryPrompt: Describe your week so far in three sentences: one point each, about real things you did.
answer: Work was busy. I finished the vendor report. On Wednesday I played badminton with friends.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Use the short word
rule: If a short word does the job, use it.

examples.work: We'll start the project on Monday.
examples.everyday: Let's start dinner. Everyone's here.

insteadOf: We will endeavour to facilitate the commencement of the project.
analogy: A key that fits the lock. A bigger key doesn't open it better.
tryPrompt: Say it simply: "We will endeavour to commence the meeting at 10."
answer: We'll start the meeting at 10.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 2; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Swap the big word
rule: Swap big words for everyday ones: "use", not "utilise".

examples.work: Please use the new portal to check your leave balance.
examples.everyday: Use the steel pan. It heats faster.

insteadOf: Please utilise the new portal to ascertain your leave balance.
analogy: Wearing a three-piece suit to buy milk. Nobody needs that much.
tryPrompt: How would you say "We need to ascertain the root cause" in everyday words?
answer: We need to find out what caused it.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 2; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Plain words land faster
rule: Plain words are easier to follow, so your idea lands faster.

examples.work: The server was set up wrong. That caused the issue.
examples.everyday: The milk went bad. Someone left it out overnight.

insteadOf: The issue is attributable to suboptimal configuration of the server.
analogy: Clear glass shows you the water. Frosted glass makes you guess.
tryPrompt: Say it plainly: "The delay is attributable to insufficient resources."
answer: We're late because we don't have enough people.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 2; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Short words for bad news
rule: When the news is bad, short words keep it clear.

examples.work: We're behind. We need two more days.
examples.everyday: I can't come. My train got cancelled.

insteadOf: We are experiencing certain challenges with respect to the timeline.
analogy: A first-aid box: plain bandages, no fancy wrapping.
tryPrompt: A task will miss its date by a week. Tell your manager in two short sentences.
answer: It'll be a week late. Testing found three big bugs.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 2; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Your turn: say it plainly
rule: Say it the way you'd tell a friend over chai.

examples.work: I'm finishing the slides now.
examples.everyday: I'm almost done. Give me ten minutes.

insteadOf: I am currently in the process of finalising the deliverables.
analogy: Like home-cooked dal: simple, and everyone enjoys it.
tryPrompt: Tell what you're working on this week in plain words, as if telling a friend.
answer: I'm building the new sign-up page. It should be done by Friday.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 2; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Say it, then stop
rule: Once your point is made, stop talking.

examples.work: Yes, it's done. I sent it at five.
examples.everyday: I'm fine with Chinese. You pick the place.

insteadOf: So yes, it's done, and like I said, it's all done now, so…
analogy: Like pouring chai: stop at the brim, or it spills.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks, "Did the client reply?" They did, and approved. Answer, then stop.
answer: Yes. They approved it this morning.

title: Say the point once
rule: Say the point once. Saying it again adds length, not strength.

examples.work: It's two days late. The new date is Thursday.
examples.everyday: The restaurant is closed. Let's try the one next door.

insteadOf: It's late. So yes, it's going to be late. Late, basically.
analogy: Honking twice at a red light doesn't make it turn green.
tryPrompt: Tell a friend you can't come to the film tonight. Say it once, with one reason.
answer: I can't make it tonight. I have an early flight.

title: Point, one reason, stop
rule: A strong short answer: the point, one reason, then stop.

examples.work: Let's use the old vendor. They've never missed a date.
examples.everyday: Let's take the metro. The roads are jammed at this hour.

insteadOf: Well, there are many reasons, one is cost, another is the team, also…
analogy: A shop sign: the name and what it sells. Nothing more.
tryPrompt: Your team asks, "Should we meet today or tomorrow?" Answer with your pick and one reason.
answer: Tomorrow. Everyone's free after ten.

title: Let them ask for more
rule: If they want the details, they'll ask. Let them.

examples.work: "Is the bug fixed?" "Yes, fixed and tested this morning."
examples.everyday: "How was the trip?" "Lovely. Goa was perfect."

insteadOf: …and I can also explain the whole history of the bug, if you want…
analogy: A shopkeeper shows one saree and waits; he doesn't unroll the whole shop.
tryPrompt: A colleague asks if you've read their email. You have. Answer in one short sentence, then stop.
answer: Yes, I read it this morning.

title: Your turn: point first, then stop
rule: Point first, short words, one idea each, then stop.

examples.work: Good day. We closed the vendor deal.
examples.everyday: A quiet Sunday. I cooked and called my parents.

insteadOf: So today, I mean, there were a lot of things, and the meeting…
analogy: A well-packed bag: only what you need, zipped shut.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "What did you get done today?" Answer about your real day: point, one reason, stop.
answer: I finished the report. It was due tomorrow, so that's a relief.

title: Cut the clutter
rule: If a word adds nothing, cut it.

examples.work: We're ready to start.
examples.everyday: Dinner's ready. Come and eat.

insteadOf: At this point in time, I would just like to basically say that we're ready to start.
analogy: Packing for a trip: anything you won't use is just weight.
tryPrompt: Cut the extra words: "At this point in time, the team is basically in agreement."
answer: Right now, the team agrees.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 3; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: One word for a long phrase
rule: Use one word where a long phrase says the same.

examples.work: We'll skip Friday's review because the deadline is close.
examples.everyday: We left early because of the Diwali traffic.

insteadOf: We'll skip Friday's review due to the fact that the deadline is close.
analogy: Taking the flyover instead of every small lane: same place, less time.
tryPrompt: Say it shorter: "In the event that it rains, we will postpone the team lunch."
answer: If it rains, we'll postpone the team lunch.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 3; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Cut the warm-up
rule: Skip the run-up line. Start with what you came to say.

examples.work: The server is down. We're on it.
examples.everyday: Your parcel came. It's with the watchman.

insteadOf: What I wanted to say was, basically, the thing is, the server is down.
analogy: Like a lift that goes straight to your floor, with no stops on the way.
tryPrompt: Cut the warm-up: "So what I'm trying to say is, the launch is moving to May."
answer: The launch is moving to May.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 3

title: Cut "actually" and "honestly"
rule: "Actually" and "honestly" rarely add meaning. Leave them out.

examples.work: I think the design is too busy.
examples.everyday: I think the blue one suits you better.

insteadOf: Actually, honestly speaking, I feel the design is too busy.
analogy: Salt in dal: a pinch helps, a fistful hides the taste.
tryPrompt: Say it cleaner: "Actually, honestly, I basically think we should wait."
answer: I think we should wait.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 3; Toastmasters Ah-Counter

title: Your turn: cut the clutter
rule: Say it, then ask yourself: which words could go?

examples.work: I finished the slides today.
examples.everyday: I finally fixed the leaking tap.

insteadOf: So basically what happened today was that I sort of finished the slides.
analogy: Weeding a garden: pull out the extras and the flowers show.
tryPrompt: Tell one thing you did today. Then say it again with three fewer words.
answer: First: "So basically I sent the client the new quote today." Then: "I sent the client the new quote."
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 3

title: Drop the hedges
rule: "Just", "maybe" and "kind of" make a clear idea sound unsure.

examples.work: I think we should try the other vendor.
examples.everyday: Let's try the new dosa place.

insteadOf: I kind of feel maybe we could probably try the other vendor.
analogy: An appeal whispered to the umpire. Say "Howzat!" like you mean it.
tryPrompt: Say it without hedges: "I was just maybe thinking we could kind of start earlier?"
answer: Can we start earlier?
credit: Smart Brevity (VandeHei, Allen & Schwartz); George Orwell (1946), rule 3

title: Ask directly
rule: Make the request in your first words, not after three softeners.

examples.work: Could you look at my email today?
examples.everyday: Can you pick up bread on your way home?

insteadOf: I just wanted to quickly check if maybe you got a chance to see it?
analogy: Ring the doorbell once, clearly, instead of tapping softly three times.
tryPrompt: How would you ask a colleague, directly and politely, to review your slides today?
answer: Could you review my slides today?
credit: Smart Brevity (VandeHei, Allen & Schwartz)

title: Polite is not the same as unsure
rule: "Please" and "could you" are polite. "Just maybe" only sounds unsure.

examples.work: Could I take Friday off? My work will be done by Thursday.
examples.everyday: Could you turn the TV down a bit, please? I'm on a call.

insteadOf: Sorry, I just maybe wanted to ask if it's possible to sort of get leave?
analogy: A soft knock is polite. Knocking and running away is just confusing.
tryPrompt: Ask your manager for a day off next week. Polite, clear, no hedges, one reason.
answer: Could I take next Monday off? I have a family event in Pune.
credit: Smart Brevity (VandeHei, Allen & Schwartz)

title: Keep one hedge when it's true
rule: If you're truly unsure, say it once, clearly.

examples.work: It should be ready by Friday. I'll confirm on Thursday.
examples.everyday: I think the shop closes at nine. Let me check.

insteadOf: It might maybe possibly be ready, I guess, probably by Friday?
analogy: Carry one umbrella if rain is likely. You don't carry five.
tryPrompt: You think the meeting room is free at 3, but you're not sure. Say it with one honest hedge.
answer: I think the room is free at 3. I'll check the booking.
credit: Smart Brevity (VandeHei, Allen & Schwartz)

title: Your turn: say it without hedges
rule: Say what you think, once, without "just" or "kind of".

examples.work: I like the plan. Let's start with the smaller city.
examples.everyday: This one's better. Let's buy it.

insteadOf: I kind of think maybe the plan is sort of okay, I guess.
analogy: A firm handshake: one clear grip, not a limp, half-hearted one.
tryPrompt: Give your real opinion on something from this week, a film, a meal or a meeting, with no hedges.
answer: The new café is great. Its filter coffee is the best near the office.
credit: Smart Brevity (VandeHei, Allen & Schwartz)

title: Pause instead of filling
rule: A short silent pause does the job of "um", more calmly.

examples.work: (Pause.) The issue is the timeline.
examples.everyday: (Pause.) I'd like the paneer tikka, please.

insteadOf: Um, so, basically, like, the thing is, the timeline is tight.
analogy: A full stop on paper. In speech, the pause is the full stop.
tryPrompt: Answer aloud: "What's the hardest part of your job?" Take a short pause before you start, in place of an "um".
answer: (Pause.) Saying no to extra work. Everything feels urgent.
credit: Toastmasters Ah-Counter; Clark & Fox Tree (2002) on "uh" and "um"

title: "Um" is normal. Fewer is the goal.
rule: Everyone says "um" sometimes. Aim for fewer, not zero.

examples.work: The report is almost done. Um, one chart is left.
examples.everyday: We'll reach around eight. Um, maybe 8:15 with traffic.

insteadOf: Um, so, um, the report, um, is, like, almost done.
analogy: One speed-breaker is fine. One every ten metres ruins the drive.
tryPrompt: Describe your morning aloud for 30 seconds. Notice your "um"s, then try again with fewer.
answer: Second try: the same story, a few "um"s fewer, with short pauses in their place.
credit: Clark & Fox Tree (2002): "uh" and "um" are real speech signals

title: Buy time with a phrase
rule: Need a second? Say "Good question" or "Let me think."

examples.work: "Why did sign-ups drop?" "Good question. Mainly the new login step."
examples.everyday: "Where should we go this weekend?" "Let me think. Maybe Lonavala?"

insteadOf: Uh, um, like, so, hmm, basically…
analogy: A batsman taking guard before the ball: a planned moment, not a panic.
tryPrompt: Someone asks, "What's your biggest goal this year?" Start with a thinking phrase, then answer.
answer: Let me think. Speaking clearly in meetings, without rambling.

title: Pause after the point
rule: After your main point, pause for one breath. Let it land.

examples.work: We launch on Monday. (Pause.) Here's what's left.
examples.everyday: I got the job. (Pause.) I start in June.

insteadOf: We're launching Monday and so yeah and also the team is…
analogy: Like the moment after a six: the crowd needs a second to cheer.
tryPrompt: Share one piece of good news from this month. Say it, pause for one breath, then add one detail.
answer: I passed my driving test. (Pause.) First try!

title: Your turn: pause, don't fill
rule: When you need a moment, pause or use a short phrase.

examples.work: (Pause.) A long day, but we fixed the payment bug.
examples.everyday: Let me think… The best part was lunch with my sister.

insteadOf: Um, so, like, my day was, um, basically fine, I guess.
analogy: A red light is a planned stop. Nobody honks at a red light.
tryPrompt: Answer "How was your day?" aloud, about your real day. Use one pause and one thinking phrase.
answer: Let me think. (Pause.) Busy, but good. I finally cleared my inbox.
credit: Toastmasters Ah-Counter; Clark & Fox Tree (2002)

title: Say who did it
rule: Name who did it: "I sent it", not "it was sent".

examples.work: I didn't send the report. I'll send it by noon.
examples.everyday: I forgot the milk. I'll get it now.

insteadOf: The report was not sent.
analogy: A CCTV clip that shows the face, not just the hand.
tryPrompt: Make it active: "It was decided to delay the launch." Say it with the person who decided.
answer: Our manager decided to delay the launch.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 4; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Own your mistakes
rule: When you got it wrong, say "I", not "it was".

examples.work: I forgot to send the client the invite. Sending it now.
examples.everyday: I broke the glass. Sorry, I'll clean it up.

insteadOf: The meeting invite was somehow not sent to the client.
analogy: A fielder who drops a catch raises his hand. Everyone knows, and play goes on.
tryPrompt: You missed a deadline for a colleague's numbers. Say it actively and give a new time.
answer: I missed the deadline on your numbers. You'll have them by three.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 4; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Give credit by name
rule: Name who did the good work, too: "Priya fixed it."

examples.work: Arjun fixed the issue over the weekend.
examples.everyday: Mum made the biryani. Dad made the raita.

insteadOf: The issue was resolved over the weekend.
analogy: Film credits name the actors, not just "a film was made".
tryPrompt: A teammate finished a hard task early. Tell your manager in one active sentence.
answer: Fatima finished the data migration two days early.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 4; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Who first, then the action
rule: Start with the person, then the action, then the thing.

examples.work: IT approved the new laptops.
examples.everyday: The plumber fixed the tap this morning.

insteadOf: Approval for the new laptops has been given by IT.
analogy: Like commentary: "Rahul drives it for four." Who, then what.
tryPrompt: Turn it around: "The new office rules were announced by HR yesterday."
answer: HR announced the new office rules yesterday.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 4; US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011)

title: Your turn: say who did it
rule: Start each sentence with who did it.

examples.work: Riya found the bug. I fixed it. Joseph released it.
examples.everyday: My brother booked the cab. I packed the snacks.

insteadOf: The bug was found, and a fix was made, and it was released.
analogy: A cooking show: you see whose hands chop the onions.
tryPrompt: Tell three things that happened at work or at home today. Start each sentence with who did it.
answer: I cleared my inbox. My manager approved the plan. My sister cooked dinner.
credit: George Orwell (1946), rule 4

title: Use the verb, not the noun
rule: Say "decided", not "made a decision". The verb is shorter.

examples.work: We analysed the data and decided on the price.
examples.everyday: We decided to go to Goa.

insteadOf: We did an analysis of the data and made a decision on the price.
analogy: A verb is the engine. A noun like "analysis" is a picture of an engine.
tryPrompt: Free the verb: "We will conduct a review of the plan on Monday."
answer: We'll review the plan on Monday.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011): avoid hidden verbs

title: Spot the hidden verb
rule: Words ending in "-tion" often hide a verb. Find it.

examples.work: We need to prepare the slides and complete the report.
examples.everyday: Let's prepare the guest list today.

insteadOf: We need to do the preparation of the slides and the completion of the report.
analogy: Like a coconut: the good part is inside the shell. Crack it open.
tryPrompt: Find the hidden verb: "Please give your confirmation of the meeting time."
answer: Please confirm the meeting time.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011): avoid hidden verbs

title: Shrink the long verb phrases
rule: "Have a discussion" becomes "discuss"; "carry out a check" becomes "check".

examples.work: Let's discuss it, then check the numbers.
examples.everyday: Let's discuss the menu before we order.

insteadOf: Let's have a discussion and then carry out a check of the numbers.
analogy: Booking an auto through three apps when you could just wave one down.
tryPrompt: Say it shorter: "Can we have a conversation about the timeline tomorrow?"
answer: Can we talk about the timeline tomorrow?
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011): avoid hidden verbs

title: Verbs make updates move
rule: In updates, lead with action verbs: fixed, sent, finished, moved.

examples.work: We finished testing. I sent the report.
examples.everyday: I booked the hall and ordered the cake.

insteadOf: The completion of testing happened, and the sending of the report is done.
analogy: A to-do list with ticks: each tick is a verb, done.
tryPrompt: Give a two-sentence update on your week. Start each sentence with "I" and a verb.
answer: I finished the deck. I booked the client demo for Friday.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011): avoid hidden verbs

title: Your turn: free the verbs
rule: Tell your day in verbs: fixed, called, cooked. Not "did the".

examples.work: Today I reviewed two designs and called the vendor.
examples.everyday: I cleaned the kitchen and called Amma.

insteadOf: Today I did the cleaning of the kitchen and made a call to Amma.
analogy: A kabaddi raid: touch, turn, run back. All action, no waiting.
tryPrompt: Tell three things you did today, at work or at home, each with a strong verb.
answer: I cleared the backlog. I called my parents. I cooked rajma for dinner.
credit: US Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011): avoid hidden verbs
